extracted.intended_audience: college instructors and curriculum developers in business communication and business education
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and delivering a unit or course to teach undergraduate business/technical/research proposal writing skills, including producing, evaluating, and defending proposals. Emphasis on both the mechanics of proposal composition and its role as planning and persuasive document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to program guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt a model proposal to the specific guidelines of the particular program under which support or approval is sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should be able to take a generic proposal model and modify it precisely to fit the format, required sections, and submission rules of the funding/approval program being targeted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate types and purposes of proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Articulate the various types of proposals and the purposes, similarities, and dissimilarities of each, and identify the major components of a research proposal, their function and criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should make students able to classify proposals (e.g., research, contract, solicited/unsolicited, technical, business, educational) and explain what each aims to accomplish and how component parts serve those aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate proposals for acceptance and writing quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate his own proposals in terms of their potential success in gaining acceptance, as well as in terms of 'correct' writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students must learn reviewer-perspective criteria: persuasiveness, feasibility, clarity, adherence to guidelines, and standard writing mechanics. Exercises: self-critiques, reviewer-role critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce full individual-initiated proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare individual-initiated proposals that contain most of the standard parts of proposals and are superior examples of effective written communication techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments should require students to draft complete proposals including problem statement, objectives/hypotheses, methodology, time schedules, budgets, personnel, and justification—written to professional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative, analytical, and intuitive thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Think creatively, analytically, intuitively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training should develop divergent and convergent thinking so students can generate feasible solutions, critique assumptions, and propose innovative approaches within realistic constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical, interesting, persuasive organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize his thoughts logically, interestingly, and persuasively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals must be structured to lead the reader through problem, rationale, methods, and benefits; rhetoric should maintain interest and make a compelling case for support.

rubrics_metrics.name: State problems and hypotheses intelligibly
rubrics_metrics.description: State problems and hypotheses in terms intelligible to those who are not sophisticated in the area of proposed research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students must learn to frame technical problems and hypotheses in clear, non-jargon language suitable for decision-makers and reviewers outside a narrow specialty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use relevant proposal vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Use intelligently the vocabulary relevant to proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate terminology (e.g., objectives, methodology, sampling, deliverables, milestones) should be used accurately and consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehend proposals and abstracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Read proposals and abstracts of research studies with understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should be able to extract aims, methods, and expected outcomes from short abstracts and full proposals, enabling informed critique and selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary methodological and measurement knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquire an elementary knowledge of sampling techniques, statistical tools, and questionnaire construction useful to the proposal writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals must demonstrate awareness of appropriate data collection and analysis methods; instruction should cover basics sufficient to design feasible studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique others' proposals constructively
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase his ability to read comprehendingly, identify weaknesses, and interpret intelligently proposals written by others and to indicate changes required for the proposal to become acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises: peer review with written critiques, reviewer role-plays. Emphasis on pointing to specific weaknesses and actionable revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciate proposal–research relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Appreciate the relationship between proposals and successful research projects; to develop a realization that the solution to a problem is normally preceded by a recognition of the problem and a 'blueprint for action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach proposals as the planning phase of research: good proposals improve eventual study quality and execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective library and information use
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the library more effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should be able to locate, synthesize, and cite secondary sources needed to justify problem significance, review literature, and support methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand nature and function of proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature and function of proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should understand what proposals are for (planning, seeking approval/funding, contracting) and how that shapes content and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand types and kinds of proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: The types and kinds of proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should distinguish among solicited vs. unsolicited, research vs. contract proposals, short informal proposals, and lengthy formal submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to principles of effective communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance of adhering to all principles of effective communication in writing proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity, conciseness, coherence, correct mechanics, appropriate tone, and audience awareness are essential; failure in these undermines persuasiveness and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize role of proposals across sectors
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of proposals in the world of business, as well as in the technological and educational spheres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should see how proposals function differently (and similarly) across domains—e.g., sales bids in business, grant requests in education, technical specs in industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify unique attributes and required procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The unique attributes of proposals and the elements and procedures required by such reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals combine persuasive argument with factual evidence and executable plans; required elements include scope, methods, resources, timeline, and budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand duties of proposal preparers
rubrics_metrics.description: The duties and responsibilities of those who prepare proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers must ensure accuracy, feasibility, ethical presentation, and alignment with sponsor requirements; they may also be responsible for follow-through if funded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish research plan from proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference between a research plan, per se, and a proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should recognize that a proposal must both plan the research and sell it—emphasizing feasibility and benefits to reviewers—not merely document methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualize proposals by scope and complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference in scope and degree of complexity which necessitates individualizing each proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form, depth, and emphasis differ for simple vs. complex projects; students must tailor length, detail, and presentation to project needs and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate procedures, resources, and constraints plausibly
rubrics_metrics.description: The complexity of articulating probable procedures, available facilities, personnel, time schedules, estimated costs, etc., into a believable, persuasive, factual, executable, interesting, attractive, and grammatically correct document that will 'sell' its reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals must balance technical accuracy with persuasive presentation; unrealistic or vague procedures and budgets undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary proposal form by complexity and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity for varying the form of proposals in line with their complexity, their length, and the readers for whom they are intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorter, less technical proposals suit managerial readers; detailed appendices and technical sections suit specialist reviewers. Teach modular writing and executive summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize proposals' function in facilitating activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of the important function proposals perform in facilitating research, problem solving, and general business activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attitudinal objective: students value proposals as tools that enable organized action and decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize broad roles of proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that proposals play an important role in various aspects of business, social, civic, political, and personal life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attitudinal: broaden students' view of where and why proposals are used, beyond academic or technical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize opportunities and responsibilities of writer
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of both the opportunities and responsibilities of the individual as a proposal writer and researcher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should see ethical and professional responsibilities: accurate claims, reasonable budgets, and respect for reviewers' time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness and desire for continued learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness of the magnitude of proposal writing, to which he has had only a brief introduction, and the development of a desire to learn more about proposal writing and to become more proficient in this aspect of communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instill curiosity and recognition that mastery requires practice and ongoing learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize proposals' contribution to advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of the contribution that proposals have made to the advancement of knowledge, the furtherance of business activity, and the solution of all kinds of problems in business management, science, education, and other areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attitudinal objective: appreciate broader societal impact of successful proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciate thorough investigation before submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Appreciation of the wisdom of thorough investigation, thought, and organization before writing and submitting proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize planning, literature review, feasibility checks, and realistic budgeting prior to drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferable communication principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Appreciation that the principles and techniques essential to acceptably-written proposals are also applicable to other forms of communication in which a writer must engage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach generalizable skills (clarity, audience awareness, organization) that benefit other workplace writing tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resilience regarding rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Appreciation that not all proposals, even though well-written, can be accepted and that, like writing for publication, a certain number of rejections must be counted on—taken in stride.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster realistic expectations and coping strategies for revision/resubmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: View comprehensive proposals as blueprint
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that comprehensive, detailed proposals serve as a blueprint or guideline for the research activity, enabling the researcher to 'stay on course toward his objective.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should learn that detailed proposals aid project management and accountability, not merely satisfy reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal as persuasive sales document (when bidding/contracts)
rubrics_metrics.description: When seeking business contracts, proposals function as sales documents: persuasive to a degree but depending heavily on factual information for competitive success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach balance between persuasive rhetoric and hard facts (costs, schedules, capabilities). Emphasize competitive positioning and compliance with solicitation terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal preparation as initial research planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal preparation is the initial planning stage of the research process; if done well it enhances chances of funding and improves the quality of the research and final report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame proposal-writing exercises as formative planning activities that reveal methodological weaknesses early and thus improve study design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical activities for skill development
rubrics_metrics.description: Use activities such as collecting and critiquing specimen proposals, preparing questionnaires, conducting group research and writing proposals, oral defense and peer critique, library assignments, and case analyses to develop proposal-writing skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific classroom tasks are recommended to teach production and evaluation skills; these also serve as authentic assessment vehicles.
